keyVerseText: Which was the son of Enos, which was the son of Seth, which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God.
rootMeaning: The Greek word Ἀδάμ (Adám) originates from the Hebrew אָדָם (ʼÂdâm), which carries the meaning of 'red' and is the name given to the first man in biblical history. This root not only identifies a historical individual but also connects to the earthiness and humanity of man, emphasizing the physical and created nature of Adam. Beyond the common English usage as a proper name, the root highlights the foundational role of Adam as the archetype of humanity, formed from the red soil of the earth.
usageInScripture: The term Ἀδάμ appears nine times in the New Testament, predominantly translated simply as 'Adam' in eight instances, with one occurrence rendered as 'which was the son of Adam.' This consistent translation underscores the word's primary function as a proper name referring to the first man. Additionally, it is used to denote 'man' in a representative sense, particularly in reference to Jesus as the last Adam, illustrating a theological link between the first man and Christ as the representative head of humanity.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding Ἀδάμ as both a historical figure and a representative man enriches the Christian comprehension of human nature and sin. Adam, as the first man, is the source from whom all humanity descends, highlighting the unity and fallen condition of mankind. The reference to Christ as the 'last Adam' reveals the redemptive plan where Jesus reverses the consequences of Adam's sin, offering new life. This word roots the doctrine of original sin and redemption in a tangible, personal figure, affirming the continuity between the Old Testament creation narrative and New Testament salvation history.
keyVerseReflection: Luke 3:38 traces Jesus' genealogy back to Adam, stating, 'which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God.' Here, Ἀδάμ serves as the pivotal link between humanity and divinity, emphasizing Jesus' true humanity as descending from the first man. This connection affirms Jesus' role as the perfect representative of mankind, while also underscoring His unique sonship of God. The use of Ἀδάμ in this verse highlights the fulfillment of God's redemptive plan through the lineage of humanity.
